Disney beats fourth-quarter estimates, targets $3 billion in savings through cost-cutting efforts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and confirmed it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.
  • Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC.
  • Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and confirmed it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

Industry observers note that "They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this tech giant," he said. "At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

Sources indicate that "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston stated. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

According to recent reports, the company will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

Sources indicate that here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The company's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

It has been revealed that disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the tech giant, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston remarked.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro said he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with newly introduced additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

"Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he stated. "And newly introduced capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

The tech giant expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

According to recent reports, over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney stated.

Sources indicate that the segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the tech giant saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney remarked Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

Sources indicate that the company expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the Latest Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

According to recent reports, D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

According to recent reports, "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro mentioned on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

Recent findings suggest that "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he said. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that plans and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

It has been revealed that the entertainment tech giant has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously confirmed a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is almost here, and for some folks, the most important part of the holiday isn't the food, family, or football. It's watching a bunch of major floats during a parade in Newly introduced York City.

OK, maybe that's not literally true, but the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an annual touchstone for lots of folks, and it's almost here. As always, there are lots of things to know about it, such as when it starts, where you can watch it, and, this year especially, whether the weather will affect the parade as expected. Let's get into it.

First and foremost, the parade starts at 8:30 a.m. ET and runs until noon on Saturday. Yes, you read that right: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is not actually on Thanksgiving Day this year. There are very good reasons for that, which we'll get to in a second.

Sources indicate that it's worth noting that, unlike most other live televised events, it will not air simultaneously in every time zone. Instead, per NBC News, it will air from 8:30 to around noon in each time zone, so no matter where you are, turn the TV on at 8:30.

The parade will air on NBC, so if you have a TV that gets local channels via cable, an antenna, or another way to watch TV, just turn on NBC.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have any of those things, Peacock will work, too. I should note that you'll need at least Peacock Premium to stream your local NBC station, and there is no free trial for that. You'll either have to pay $12.99 per month or borrow someone else's login. According to NBC News, this year's parade will feature 100 inflatables in total, the most they've ever used for one of these. You can see the full balloon lineup on the Macy's website, but rest assured that all your favorites are likely included, like Sonic the Hedgehog and the Pink Panther. There are also new ones, like a DoorDash float and a GEICO float. One float will also act as a tribute of sorts for Fiona the hippo, which is nice.

Sources indicate that performers include Teddy Swims and Megan Moroney on the main stage, with other floats featuring acts such as the Baha Men, Blues Traveler, Icona Pop, and Devo. There's a little something for everyone.

And now for the bad news: There's a weather system moving up the East Coast that has caused the parade organizers to reschedule it this year, per NBC News.

Industry observers note that two storms combined into one in the American South, with the result expected to bring wind gusts of up to 45mph to Newly introduced York City starting on Thursday morning. This is a problem because the city has an upper limit of 34mph for gusts regarding massive inflatable objects. The parade was still scheduled for Thursday until the middle of Wednesday afternoon, when organizers and New York City officials decided to push it back to Saturday.

Unfortunately, that means you'll need a initiative B for Thursday morning entertainment, but, more importantly, this should keep everyone who planned to attend the parade on Thursday safe.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Video's newly introduced "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

Sources indicate that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over.".

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

In a recent development, "We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion.".

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey.".

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

It has been revealed that "You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

Industry observers note that "There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”.

It has been revealed that "Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0).

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

Sources indicate that the question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

In a recent development, mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late 1700s (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

Recent findings suggest that in Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, notes maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

If true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” indicates Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis.

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing new techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

It has been revealed that riemann then indicated that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since its introduction in 2018, Hinge's "Most Compatible" feature has earned equal parts praise and scorn from online daters, who can't seem to decide if it's the best thing ever or a bad joke.

Even today, eight years after it was first introduced, Most Compatible is a marvel of mathematical engineering, beginning with its foundation: the Gale-Shapley algorithm (also known as the propose-and-reject algorithm), developed all the way back in 1962 to solve a (hypothetical) mating problem.

According to recent reports, hinge's variation of the algorithm works dynamically, constantly taking into account user preferences and choices to predict what kind of person you would most like to date. At the start of each new day, you will receive a Most Compatible profile suggestion that expires after 24 hours unless you interact with it.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

According to recent reports, but there's a massive catch here that too many Hinge customers are unaware of: your own actions and inactions are factored into the equation, so if you feed the algorithm bad data, it won't work in your favor, and you'll rarely see a compelling profile suggestion. We reached out to Hinge to gain a better understanding of their algorithm from the inside, and they described it as a "recommendation system" that combines multiple algorithms, "using your stated preferences and your activity on the app," to adjust and refine its suggestions.

Here are three key tips from Hinge to help its recommendation algorithm work for you:.

Too many Hinge users (and men in particular!) cast a wide net, interacting with as many profiles as possible, sending out Likes all over the place. We get it: the more-is-more approach has its appeal, but it actually hurts the algorithm's effectiveness, since it becomes harder to narrow down your preferences when you're too indiscriminate about who you like or interact with.

Or, as Hinge told us: "If you send too many likes, we can’t tell what you truly want. At the same time, if you rarely send likes, we don’t have enough information to learn from about who excites you. By engaging with others with curiosity and purpose, your recommendations meaningfully evolve alongside you.".

Instead of being overly enthusiastic in your search, be intentional: take your time to vet profiles and interact only with people you can genuinely see yourself dating. You may not even necessarily know what these profiles might have in common, but rest assured the algorithm will be at work in the background finding the common thread and refining its suggestions for you in the future.

Industry observers note that the default Hinge filters are very relaxed, but there's actually a Dealbreakers toggle hidden in the Dating Preferences section of your profile. The normal preferences (location and age range, for example) are taken into account but treated more like guidelines than hard limits. However, if you start enabling your Dealbreakers, Hinge will treat them as hard limits and never even show you profiles that don't match your preferences. As Hinge put it to us, "Hinge will only show you each other if you both meet the dealbreakers that either of you set, such as wanting kids. This helps you focus on people who feel like a real long-term match.".

Most dating app consumers, out of sheer eagerness to start browsing local singles, make a half-hearted attempt to fill out their profiles, usually doing the bare minimum to meet the app's requirements. But Hinge offers an extremely generous array of profile fields, and the more you fill out, the more data the algorithm can use to do its matchmaking work.

Industry observers note that and as Hinge pointed out to us, not answering a question is treated like a negative, actively shrinking your dating pool: "When you select 'prefer not to say,' it limits who can see you. From family plans and dating intentions to drinking habits, you're excluded from being shown to people who've set Dealbreakers around those compatibility factors.".

We recommend you put particular focus on filling out Hinge's prompts in a thoughtful way, taking particular care to choose ones that reflect directly on your personality or interests.

According to recent reports, in Hinge's own profile guide, they offer vital advice that is too often overlooked: ditch the clichés and one-word or low-effort responses, and take the time to give a personal answer to every question. And take the time to answer a voice prompt, as you'll be rewarded by the algorithm for doing so.

Finally, there's good evidence that Hinge's algorithm rewards profiles with refreshed photos, so if you haven't updated your main photos in a minute, follow their photo refresh guide to optimize your upcoming pics.

If you follow the steps above, you should start to see the algorithm working more in your favor, and you'll look forward to each day's new Most Compatible suggestion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute for Birmingham City against Manchester United on Sunday.

After 13 months away, Simone Magill made her return to football as a late substitute in Birmingham City's WSL defeat by Manchester United on Sunday.

It was a moment that had been a long time coming for the 31-year-old, who gave birth to her daughter, Skye, in May and has been building towards stepping back on the pitch.

Now, she will hope to make her international return with Northern Ireland in a friendly against Greece on Friday.

"It's been some time since I've been here in a playing capacity, so it's really nice just to be back in the mix again," NI captain Magill told BBC Sport NI.

"I officially made my comeback at the weekend and it was really nice to have done that. I'm really looking forward to doing that here at home in front of the fans and my family as well.".

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'.

Greece friendlies an opportunity to build - Andrews.

In an interview with BBC Sport in October, Magill spoke about how being both a mum and a footballer can "co-exist".

While she was not ready to play any role in the matches, Magill, Skye and her husband Mark were all in camp for the World Cup play-off with Portugal last month, all with an eye of integrating into international duty as a family.

Having played just a handful of minutes, Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle noted that while he was "delighted" to have Magill back, how much she plays across the double-header would be in collaboration with Birmingham and his captain.

"With the circumstances around this one, I'm very mindful that I need to build accordingly and I really need to listen to myself as well," Magill added.

"To even be back in this capacity this soon after giving birth, for me, is just unbelievable.

In a recent development, "I have no major expectations. I'm just really happy to be here and be a part of it, and if I do come on, that'll be even better.".

Friday, 27 November at 19:00 GMT.

Watch live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website.

Friday's match against Greece will be Northern Ireland's first friendly in three years.

The sides will then play again on Tuesday at 16:00 GMT, and both matches can be streamed live on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport app and website.

The matches will act as preparation for the Nations League campaign in February, when Northern Ireland face tricky tests in the form of Poland, Finland and Belarus.

McArdle is developing a young squad and Magill says she hopes to bring "leadership and experience to really help us all move forward".

"We've obviously had a transition in the last year whilst I've been out, it's been nice to come back in and just feel where we're at, get on the grass with the girls and see, 'how can I help, what can I bring?'," she added.

"I'm very much looking forward to just getting back in the mix and helping try to bring the young players forward, use that experience and let's hold on to the ball, let's get into the final third, let's have a go, be brave - all of the attributes that we're known for.

"We're an underdog nation, so it's getting that across to the younger members in the squad to say, 'let's have a go with these teams and not be afraid'.".

Simone Magill (centre) is set to make her Northern Ireland return against Greece.

In her absence over the past year, Northern Ireland have used a number of different options in the centre forward role.

Winger Lauren Wade has shown her versatility by playing centrally, while Kess Elmore and Cora Chambers have also played up top.

Along with Magill, Portsmouth striker Kerry Beattie is also back in the squad to bolster McArdle's striking options.

"We've loads of young ones snapping at my heels. It's great, that's what we want.

Industry observers note that "I feel we're more competitive now than ever. You never know who's going to be coming into the squad. Certainly, in more recent years, you kind of knew the squad every single time, whereas that's not the case now.

"We've got some exciting youth coming through, so it's their time now to shine.".

Magill added that Northern Ireland are "heading in a fresh direction" ahead of the Nations League campaign next year, and the friendlies with Greece give an opportunity for the team to grow in a pressure-free environment.

"We're coming into a brand new campaign and it's really nice that we have a friendly window just now.

"We haven't had one in a very, very long time, so this is a brilliant opportunity to get us all back together, get the new faces in, get some more experience, learn things, try things.

"I'm really excited about where we're going.".

This blog is now closed. Read below for more on these stories and all other things Germany on Monday, November 23.

Thank you for following our coverage of headlines from Germany on Monday, November 24.

In a recent development, the Federal President’s latest major trip takes him to Africa. Frank-Walter Steinmeier has just visited the Ivory Coast and is continuing on to Ghana and Kenya. His goal: to encourage more German companies to invest in Africa.

In a recent development, frank-Walter Steinmeier has visited 31 African countries during his political career. Even as foreign minister, he traveled regularly to the continent; as federal president, he has made twelve trips so far.

From early on, he viewed Africa not only through the lens of development aid and humanitarian support, but also — much like former Chancellor Angela Merkel — as a market for the German economy that has been underutilized thus far. In 2015, as foreign minister in the Merkel administration, Steinmeier played a central role in the creation of the German-African Economic Summit.

On his current trip as well, Steinmeier is advocating for greater German engagement in Africa. In Abidjan, the capital of the Ivory Coast, following a meeting with Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara, he called on German companies to step outside their comfort zone and take greater advantage of the opportunities offered by the country and the continent.

The Ivory Coast is considered a location with growing potential. Despite its proximity to the Sahel region, which is plagued by terrorism, the country is relatively stable politically. The economy is growing by about six percent annually. Germany has more intensive trade relations with the Ivory Coast than with any other country in sub-Saharan Africa, and nowhere else in sub-Saharan Africa do so many people learn German — an advantage for German small and medium-sized enterprises — all of which both presidents emphasized very clearly during their meeting in Abidjan.

Up next, Steinmeier is scheduled to visit Accra, Ghana, for the sixth German-African Economic Summit, where more than 600 business representatives are expected to attend. As the summit’s initiator, the Federal President will open the event together with the host, Ghanaian President John Mahama. He will be accompanied by a ten-member business delegation representing industry, the financial sector, and energy consulting.

Recent findings suggest that the Economic Summit is taking place at a time when Germany’s relations with African countries are undergoing fundamental changes. In light of geopolitical shifts, Africa is increasingly coming into focus as an economic and trade partner.

According to recent reports, the continent’s share of German foreign trade at the moment stands at just under 2%, or around €30 billion. At the same time, German exports to Africa are rising by at least 6% annually. And since Germany’s economy aims to reduce its dependence on China in the future, opportunities in Africa are growing.

From Ghana, Frank-Walter Steinmeier will travel on to Kenya, the final stop on his tour of Africa.

Environment Minister Carsten Schneider on Monday vowed that Germany will continue to move away from burning fossil fuels despite the failure of the COP31 declaration in Antalya, Turkey, this weekend.

Speaking at an event in Potsdam, Schneider noted: "We will clearly maintain our course on climate protection in Europe and Germany, but above all one that makes us independent of oil and gas because otherwise we are vulnerable to blackmail and our economic performance becomes extremely volatile.".

Schneider expressed disappointment less at the result of the two-week conference than its format, which he said was far more focussed on spectacle than substance.

Industry observers note that speaking of his vision for a format for future climate conferences, Schneider noted: "Basically, I don't need so many people there. What I need are the relevant decision makers with whom I negotiate and make decisions.".

Although he voiced relief that the final document from the conference had not represented a step backwards — as well as stressing that some 30 countries had pledged to maintain the move away from fossil fuels — Schneider acknowledged that it had been nearly impossible to find consensus with Russia and Saudi Arabia at the table.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius urged calm over reports that Russia was planning to launch a nuclear-armed satellite into space as early as next month.

"First of ​all, ‌let's remain calm, because there are reports — that's true — but ‌it's ​not clear what kind of weapons these are, and the ​effect they might have depends, in ⁠turn, ​on where they ​are deployed," Pistorius told ​reporters in ‌Berlin.

"Therefore, it's too early to ​speculate ⁠publicly about this. We are consulting ⁠internally ​and taking the necessary measures.".

German public broadcasters NDR and WDR and newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung first reported on the matter, which mentioned that internal intelligence reports circulated among NATO countries earlier this month said that Russia was ready to bring the alleged satellite, named Sputnik-S, out of storage in Moscow.

The reports said Russia may be planning to launch it as soon as December.

Nuclear weapons are banned in orbit by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, of which Moscow is a signatory.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz mentioned not allowing Ukraine intoNATO in 2008 was a mistake.

At the2008 summit in Bucharest, Romania, German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy argued that they weren't ready to extend NATO membership to Ukraine.

According to recent reports, US President George W. Bush mentioned he was in favor of having Ukraine enter into NATO.

But both Germany and France remarked that that would hurt relations with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The NATO summit then decided that Ukraine would eventually join the alliance, but offered no timetable.

At a press conference on Monday, Merz was asked about whether he thinks the time was right to talk about Ukraine's membership in NATO.

To which Merz mentioned, "If it [Ukraine] had become a member of NATO, this war could probably have been prevented.".

Merz meant Russia's war against Ukraine when he remarked "this war" at the press conference after a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Angela Merkel defended her decision at the Bucharest summit as of 2024 as well, saying a large proportion of the Ukrainian population had opposed joining NATO at the time.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

In a recent development, "Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz noted.

Merz stated Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

German startup investments in fields such as robotics and defense are set to almost triple this year, a study noted on Monday.

The German Start-up Association and the Joachim Herz Foundation study predicted that investments in so-called "deep tech startups" will surge from just €2.9 billion ($3.17 billion) last year to 8.1 billion ($8.9 billion) this year.

The study described the rise as a "major success for Germany as a business location.".

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

The study also showed about 300 latest deep tech startups are expected to be founded this year, a 40% rise compared with last year.

Newly found startups tend to be founded around economic hubs like Berlin and Hamburg, which are also home to leading universities and research institutes.

The study also highlighted challenges, including limited funding compared with their US counterparts and insufficient support to move startups from the laboratory to the real world.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

They said that while they were investigating the claims, they did not initially have reason to treat them as credible threats.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

Read more about the disruptive incidents that have targeted Europe in recent weeks.

Germany's Freie Wähler (Free Voters) party have chosen a new chairman, weeks after their former front man Hubert Aiwanger unexpectedly passed away on November 4.

According to recent reports, the party declared on Monday that Bavaria's Digital Affairs Fabian Mehring is to succeed Aiwanger both as party leader on the federal level and as one of two co-chairs of the Bavaria section of they party. The second state co-chair still needs to be decided.

Aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Industry observers note that there are also changes in the Bavarian state government. Tobias Gotthardt is to take over as economy minister, while Environment Minister Thorsten Glauber is set to become deputy premier behind Bavaria state Premier Markus Söder. The appointments still require formal approval by party conventions.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has inisted that NATO was ready to defend itself in the face of potential Russian threats against any of its member states.

"We will always defend every inch of our NATO territory," Wadephul said at the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

His comments come after three Russian projectiles violated Polish airspace on Friday and crashed in the southeast of the country.

Wadephul is attending the NATO assembly in Berlin and DW has   a dedicated blog on those talks  where you can read all about how Russia's war in Ukraine is taking center stage for the defense alliance.

Industry observers note that A massive strike is underway in Germany hitting major car brands another manufacturing factors. Metal and electrical workers are demanding better pay ahead of upcoming wage talks later this week. The strike has been initiated by IG Metall, Germany’s biggest and most powerful union.

Famous car brands Mercedes and BMW  were affected as was an Opel plant, which is part of the international Stellantis group.

The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

The tough struggle over wages comes as especially the German car industry is facing serious headwinds because of higher energy prices, US tariffs and mounting Chinese competition.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.

It mentioned that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report noted the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin said the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

In a recent development, german exports to Africa have reached a latest record. That’s according to a fresh study just as the country's president embarks on a trip to several African countries.

Exports are expected to rise by 6% in 2026 to reach about 30 billion euros ($33bn).

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

The biggest single export at the moment is a high-speed train network to Egypt. Other main exports include electrical equipment, optical instruments, plastics and pharmaceuticals, as well as food products, including dairy goods, cereals and baked goods.

The data is being reported by the Reuters news agency, based on the government-owned agency Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI), which promotes foreign trade and investment in Germany.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider noted after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention intends to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that "I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider mentioned.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

Industry observers note that he begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems.
  • Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Establishing a permanent human presence on the Moon will require more than rockets, habitats, and life support systems. Engineers must also find ways to protect astronauts and equipment from extreme temperatures that can swing from hundreds of degrees below zero to boiling hot. Reliable insulation will be essential, but keeping heat under control is only part of the problem.

Materials used in lunar construction must also survive transportation, installation, accidental impacts, and years of handling. Many of the best insulators are surprisingly delicate, making them poorly suited to the demanding conditions of a working Moon base.

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Pennsylvania may have found an answer in an unexpectedly familiar material: Mylar. This lightweight plastic is used in everyday products such as food wrap and, when coated with aluminum, the reflective emergency blankets that help marathon runners retain body heat. By arranging hundreds of extremely thin Mylar sheets into carefully designed stacks, the team has created insulation that remains effective even after being bent or subjected to intense pressure.

It has been revealed that the research, published in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces, introduces a material known as hybrid layered insulating film stacks (HyLIFS). Its main advantage is the ability to combine two qualities that are difficult to achieve together: excellent thermal insulation and resistance to physical damage.

"These stacks of Mylar can bend, withstand substantial compression and maintain their insulating performance," notes senior author Igor Bargatin, Associate Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM), "potentially allowing them to be packed, transported and survive rough treatment over many years of use.".

If engineers can eventually manufacture the material on a large scale, it could be used to protect lunar habitats, spacesuits, and other equipment designed to function for extended periods in the vacuum of space.

Sources indicate that "The combination of thermal and mechanical robustness is critical for long-term use on the Moon," notes first author Danielle R. Levin, a recent Penn doctoral graduate in chemistry, who also received a master's in MEAM. "This material could open a pathway to inexpensive, durable and reusable lunar insulation.".

Why Moon Bases Need Tougher Insulation.

Sources indicate that designing insulation for the Moon involves a difficult balancing act. A material must slow the movement of heat through a vacuum while also remaining strong enough to withstand the stresses of everyday use.

It has been revealed that some existing materials are outstanding at preventing heat transfer but offer little protection against physical damage. Aerogels, for instance, consist mostly of empty space, which makes them extremely lightweight and effective at retaining heat. They have been used in applications ranging from industrial pipelines to NASA's Mars rovers. However, their delicate internal structure can make them vulnerable to impacts and compression.

It has been revealed that another widely used space technology, multilayer insulation, relies on reflective sheets separated by insulating spacers. It works particularly well at reducing heat transfer through radiation, but it is not intended to support substantial weight. Even routine contact can cause tearing or other damage.

Strengthening insulation often creates another problem: the changes that make it more durable can also allow more heat to pass through. For future lunar infrastructure, engineers need a material that can resist damage without sacrificing thermal performance.

"For lunar infrastructure, we would ideally like both," says Bargatin. "The ideal material is both resistant to damage and to the loss of heat.".

How Ordinary Mylar Became Powerful Space Insulation.

According to recent reports, the Penn researchers focused on Mylar, a well-known plastic formally called biaxially oriented polyethylene terephthalate, or BoPET. Already used extensively in aerospace technology, the polymer is also found in the lightweight emergency blankets distributed after marathons. Adding a metallic coating such as aluminum allows Mylar to reflect infrared radiation, helping prevent heat from escaping.

It has been revealed that rather than relying on a single sheet, the researchers investigated what would happen if many thin layers were stacked together. They experimented with different film thicknesses and applied extremely thin coatings of aluminum oxide, also called alumina, to some samples to make the sheets stiffer.

It has been revealed that assembling the experimental stacks was surprisingly difficult. Each delicate film had to be positioned individually, requiring painstaking manual work.

"At the moment, the process is very time-consuming," notes Levin. "We use two pairs of tweezers and small weights to handle and stack the delicate films. Even breathing near the stack can send the layers flying.".

Despite the simplicity of the basic idea, testing revealed an impressive combination of properties. In a vacuum, the best stacks achieved thermal conductivity comparable to other advanced vacuum insulation materials while retaining their flexibility.

The researchers also tested the material under compression similar to what insulation could experience inside a lunar habitat, where the interior air pressure would push against walls exposed to the vacuum outside.

Additional mechanical testing demonstrated that stacks coated with alumina could tolerate the greatest compressive stresses available with the laboratory equipment while maintaining their insulating performance. The results demonstrated that improving durability did not necessarily require giving up thermal protection.

Crushing Pressure Reveals Unexpected Durability.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most striking findings came when the team subjected the material to repeated compression. Even the researchers were surprised by how well the thin plastic layers held up.

The samples were compressed to approximately 20 megapascals, a pressure comparable to concentrating 200 pounds of force onto an area the size of a fingertip. Instead of testing the material only once, the researchers repeated the process 10 times.

"We were concerned about the material failing under such high compressive stress," recalls Levin. "But the stacks didn't survive just one high stress cycle -- they survived 10 in a row.".

This resistance to damage could be especially valuable for lunar exploration. Every piece of equipment needed on the Moon must first endure the challenges of being packed, debuted, transported, and installed. Insulation that can bend, withstand pressure, and potentially be reused would offer significant practical advantages.

According to recent reports, durability would remain notable after construction is complete. Astronauts living and working inside a lunar habitat could accidentally strike or compress insulation during maintenance or ordinary activities.

"You could use these stacks to insulate a lunar habitation, but astronauts will inevitably have little accidents where they bump into them," notes Bargatin. "When we're talking about long-term habitation on the moon, it's really important to have tough materials that can last long enough.".

Tiny Particles Reveal a Hidden Secret of Heat Transfer.

Beyond demonstrating the material's durability, the experiments uncovered an important clue about how heat travels through layers of Mylar.

According to recent reports, the discovery involved microscopic particles already present in commercially manufactured plastic films. Extremely thin sheets naturally tend to stick to one another and to nearby surfaces, which complicates manufacturing and handling. To prevent this, producers add tiny "antiblocking" particles that extend slightly above the plastic surface and keep neighboring sheets from clinging together.

Although manufacturers have long understood why these particles are useful, their influence on heat transfer in stacked Mylar films had received relatively little attention.

Traditional multilayer space insulation is primarily designed to control heat transferred by radiation. As a result, researchers have had less reason to investigate how small points of physical contact between films might affect heat conduction.

The Penn team examined this possibility by constructing mathematical models of heat transfer between individual layers and comparing the predictions with laboratory measurements.

The findings indicate that, in a vacuum, much of the heat moving from one Mylar sheet to the next passes through the tiny contact points created by the antiblocking particles.

That result could have important implications for future insulation design. Instead of accepting the particles as an incidental feature of commercial plastic, engineers might deliberately control their size, abundance, and placement to reduce unwanted heat transfer.

Why Thinner Plastic Does Not Always Insulate Better.

The role of these microscopic particles also helped explain another unexpected result.

According to recent reports, at first, the researchers assumed that thinner Mylar sheets would produce better insulation. Using thinner films would allow more layers to occupy the same amount of space, increasing the number of boundaries that heat must cross.

However, the experiments did not fully support that expectation. When coated with alumina, the thinnest films the team successfully characterized provided thermal performance similar to films of medium thickness.

The researchers suspect that the antiblocking particles help explain why. In thinner sheets, the particles can produce more contact between adjacent layers, creating additional routes for heat to move through the material. Those extra contact points can offset the expected advantages of adding more layers.

In a recent development, the finding suggests that making films thinner is not automatically the best approach. Engineers must also consider how the sheets bend and deform under pressure, along with the number and arrangement of microscopic contact points.

Industry observers note that "As you compress the layers, the contact landscape changes," indicates Levin. "It's not just a matter of minimizing the film thickness or the number of particles; we must also account for how the contacts change and the films deform as pressure increases.".

Ultimately, the ability of these stacks to limit heat transfer depends on several interacting factors, including the thickness and stiffness of the plastic and the distribution of particles within it.

From Tiny Laboratory Samples to Future Moon Bases.

Although the early results are encouraging, the new insulation is still far from being ready for lunar construction.

Recent findings suggest that the experimental HyLIFS samples presently measure only about one square centimeter, and producing them requires hours of careful cutting and manual stacking. That painstaking process would be impractical for manufacturing the large sheets needed to insulate an entire habitat.

In a recent development, to make the material useful on a larger scale, the researchers will need a more efficient production method. One possibility involves continuously applying coatings to large rolls of Mylar, using manufacturing techniques that could eventually produce sheets measured in meters rather than centimeters.

Such an approach might also allow engineers to adjust the thickness of the plastic, the protective coatings, and the distribution of antiblocking particles before assembling the material into larger stacks.

According to recent reports, vital questions remain. The researchers still need to determine whether large versions of the material will retain the same insulating properties and mechanical strength seen in the laboratory. Further testing must also establish how well the stacks tolerate repeated bending, accidental impacts, scratches, and other wear associated with real-world use.

If those challenges can be overcome, the technology could provide lightweight, flexible, durable insulation for lunar habitats, rovers, electronic equipment, and other systems operating in space.

For Levin, the results also offer a broader lesson about materials engineering. Even familiar products can reveal unexpected capabilities when researchers examine how their structures behave under different conditions.

"The simplest configuration ended up being the best one," she states.

The research was carried out at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science (Penn Engineering). Additional co-authors include Matthew F. Campbell, Gulzhan Aldan, and Orevaoghene H. Omodior.

Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation Division of Chemical, Bioengineering, Environmental and Transport Systems (grant number 1845933) and Penn Engineering.

Latest Update: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Navy debuted the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.
  • Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.
  • After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy debuted the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were rolled out.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was introduced by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds.".

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that debuted two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced newly introduced restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.
  • The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced newly introduced restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have revealed curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

In a recent development, last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it mentioned, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based firm had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it mentioned last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#208298. A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • Recent findings suggest that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a upcoming way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

Sources indicate that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results showed that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

Recent findings suggest that the experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

Recent findings suggest that the second state was particularly vital because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

According to recent reports, "This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

Sources indicate that the discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely newly introduced electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

Sources indicate that future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open fresh possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

Whats newly introduced to streaming this week? (Nov. 27, 2026)
